newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW - Market awakens but still yawning.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Market awakens but still yawning.

text.p: The IPO market, slowly emerging from its holiday slumber, offers slim pickings this week and will only get into gear toward the end of the month.
"There's not even wing-flapping," John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket, said of the outlook for the week. "The flying will start after that."
And in the face of broader market volatility, investors are going to be flying into the IPO market more cautiously than they did at this time last year, analysts said.

The Dow continued its gyrations last week, hitting four record highs. On Friday it fell 70 points early in the day, triggered by strong employment data, but staged a late rally to reach a peak of 6704 at the close.

Steve Harmon, senior investment analyst at Mecklermedia's iWorld, said that as secondary markets grapple with conflicting economic signals and interest rate jitters, good balance sheets and positive earnings will drive the success of new offerings.
"You're taking a company to market, not a concept," he said.

Ryan Jacob, director of research at the IPO Value Monitor, agreed. "It's not the same kind of environment we saw in the first half of '96," he said. "Institutional investors are going to be very hesitant to buy into just a 'concept.'"
Manish Shah of the IPO Maven is skeptical about an IPO market more focused on fundamentals. "I don't see, and don't expect, any improvement in quality" over last year, he said.
He does, however, expect the 1997 market to differ from the 1996 market in that it will see more IPOs that are spin-offs of conglomerates.

Peter Doyle, co-director of the Spin-Off Report, echoed this view. Diversified companies are seeking to enhance shareholder value by restructuring because "the marketplace is paying higher multiples for more focused companies," he said.

Shah said 1997 should also see a lower volume of IPO deals -- about 500 versus last year's 800 or so -- because "if the broader markets don't advance as much, not as many companies will come to market."
But given the number of deals currently in registration, IPO volume should return to the levels of last October-November over the next few months, said Jacob.
Conspicuously in the pipeline are many medical and biotechnology companies, which were enjoying a resurgence after being among the worst performers in last year's IPO market, he said.
For the week, analysts see little to write home about. The biggest deal is Transcrypt International Inc TRII.O, which could see a small premium at its opening, according to Fitzgibbon.
The Lincoln, Neb.-based company provides information security products that prevent unauthorized access to sensitive voice and data communications.
Transcrypt is offering 3.75 million shares at an estimated $12 to $14 per share. The lead underwriter is Dain Bosworth Inc.
Also of some interest, said analysts, is Aramex International Ltd, a Middle Eastern company that provides express delivery and freight forwarding services.
Aramex is offering one million shares at $7 to $8 a share in a deal led by Commonwealth Associates.
Fitzgibbon sees a premium of about 3/8 point on the deal.
